notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Genesis 44, drawn from the permitted sites.

---

## GENESIS 44 — VERSE-BY-VERSE NOTES

### v. 1 — Joseph commands his steward to fill the sacks and return the money.

**Traditional Reading:** Joseph ordered the steward to fill the brothers' sacks "as much as they can carry" — an act of generosity. The return of the money this second time was, according to Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, partly from "kindly feelings to his father" and partly to prevent suspicion falling on Benjamin alone: if the cup were found in Benjamin’s sack but money in everyone’s, all would appear equally innocent of theft, though Benjamin would face greater trouble. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/genesis/44.htm)

Gill adds that Joseph commanded this "out of his great affection for them, and that his father and his family might have sufficient supply in this time of famine." The money returned was what they had just paid for the present corn, not the previous trip's money (which the steward had already acknowledged receiving). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-44.html)

---

### v. 2 — The silver cup placed in Benjamin's sack.

**Traditional Reading:** The "cup" (Hebrew *gabia‘*) denotes a large goblet or bowl, not an ordinary drinking cup (*kos*). Ellicott says it was "a large round vessel from which the wine was poured into the drinking cups." The Cambridge Bible notes the word suggests a vessel "shaped like the calyx of a flower." Gill describes it as "a large embossed cup… a kind of goblet" — valuable both for its silver material and for being Joseph's personal drinking vessel. Joseph did not reveal his intention to the steward — he simply gave the order and it was carried out. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/44.htm; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/genesis/44.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-44.html)

The Pulpit Commentary notes that this was not a repeat of the earlier test (the money-in-sacks of ch.42); this time the test was brought "to a point by associating Benjamin with the loss of the cup." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/44.htm)

**Modern Scholarship (Constable):** The Hebrew *gabia‘* refers to a chalice or goblet, not a common cup. The brothers inferred Joseph used it for more than drinking — likely for divination, which enhanced its perceived value and the seriousness of its theft. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-44.html)

---

### v. 3 — The brothers depart at daybreak.

**Traditional Reading:** Gill notes the brothers were "handsomely and honourably dismissed" — refreshed with food, their donkeys fed and loaded. They left in high spirits: Simeon was released, sacks were full, and they had been feasted by the Egyptian governor (Genesis 43:32-34). Everything appeared well. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-44.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-44/)

---

### vv. 4–5 — Joseph sends his steward to pursue and accuse.

**Traditional Reading on the test:** Enduring Word (David Guzik) emphasizes that Joseph was not taking revenge. "Guided by the hand of God, Joseph tested the hearts of his brothers, and the process would bring them to complete repentance." The question "Why have you repaid evil for good?" highlighted base ingratitude — they had been feasted and honoured, yet (supposedly) stole their host's prized cup. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-44/)

**On the divination claim ("whereby indeed he divineth"):** This verse is one of the most debated in the chapter. The traditional commentators generally agree Joseph himself did **not** practice pagan divination:

- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** "It is not likely that Joseph, a pious believer in the true God, would have addicted himself to this superstitious practice. But he might have availed himself of that popular notion to carry out the successful execution of his stratagem." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/genesis/44.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "No reason to suppose that Joseph actually used this art. It would have been inconsistent with his habitual faithfulness to God… He was now acting a part. He spoke in the character of an Egyptian ruler." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/44.htm)
- **Enduring Word:** "It is possible (though not likely) that Joseph also did this, because there was not yet specific revelation from God that such a practice was forbidden. The point was to make the brothers aware that this was a special cup, and it was a terrible crime to steal it." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-44/)

**Ellicott takes a different view:** He says cup-divination (hydromancy) was common in Egypt — a kind of clairvoyance where one gazed into a water-filled bowl until a half-stupor state was induced. "In Genesis 44:15, Joseph asserts that he practised this art, and innocently. Though used now generally for imposture, there is in clairvoyance a real physical basis, which would be inexplicable in an unscientific age; and the genuine piety and goodness of Joseph would not raise him above the reach of the superstitions of his time." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/44.htm)

**Constable (Evangelical/Scholarly):** The Hebrew verb in v.5 and v.15 is *naḥash* ("to whisper, mumble formulations, prophesy"), not *qasam* (the normal word for "to divine"). Leon Wood believed Joseph meant he had information not available to ordinary people. Constable notes some interpreters (Waltke, Mathews) believe Joseph's claim was just part of the ruse. "The first statement made by Joseph's servant may have been a lie (44:5). The second statement made by Joseph did not claim to practice divination (44:15)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-44.html)

---

### vv. 6–10 — The brothers protest their innocence and make a rash oath.

**Traditional Reading:** The brothers' confident reply — "Far be it from us that your servants should do such a thing" — reveals, as Guzik notes, a healthy trust among them. "If they did not trust each other, they would have immediately wondered which brother stole the cup." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-44/)

They point to their proven honesty: they brought back the money found in their sacks on the first trip. Gill observes: "If they would not retain the governor's money when in their own land and out of his reach, much less would they steal anything out his house." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-44.html)

Their oath ("let him die, and we also will be my lord's slaves") was rash — both Gill and Constable note this. Constable points out the parallel with Jacob's rash oath when Laban searched for his teraphim hidden in Rachel's tent (Genesis 31:32-35): "Now the Egyptians searched for Joseph's cup of divination and found it in the sack of Benjamin, Rachel's son." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-44.html)

The steward wisely moderates: only the guilty one becomes a slave; the rest go free. Constable observes: "Joseph had set his brothers up with a perfect excuse to abandon Benjamin and free themselves from slavery." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-44.html)

---

### vv. 11–13 — The search and discovery; the brothers tear their clothes.

**Traditional Reading:** Each man "speedily" lowered his sack — they were certain of innocence. The steward searched "beginning with the oldest and left off with the youngest." Gill explains this method was used "partly to hold them in fear as long as he could, and partly to prevent any suspicion of design, which might have been entertained had he went directly to Benjamin's sack." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-44.html)

When the cup was found, "they tore their clothes" — an expression of extreme horror, as if someone had died. Constable notes: "They tore their clothes in anguish, as Jacob had done when he received news of Joseph's apparent death (Genesis 37:34)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-44.html)

Enduring Word highlights the transformation: "Before, they didn't care about their father or his favored son. Now, the idea of hurting either father or son made them feel as bad as if someone had died." They all returned to the city together — when Joseph was taken as a slave, they allowed him to go; now they stood with Benjamin. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-44/)

Constable quotes Mathews: "That all the brothers suffered such distress is a telling sign of the new sense of unity they had developed… The brothers are of one accord without any grumbling or dissent. … They were guilty [previously] but did not show remorse; now they are innocent and demonstrate deepest agony." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-44.html)

---

### vv. 14–15 — The brothers return and bow before Joseph.

**Traditional Reading:** The brothers fell before Joseph "on the ground" — Guzik notes this is the third time they fulfilled Joseph's prophetic dreams (Genesis 37:5-11). "They had been wronged, and the evidence against them had been planted. Yet they didn't come demanding justice, but with a humble plea for mercy." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-44/)

Joseph's question — "Do you not know that a man like me can surely divine the truth?" — continues the persona of an Egyptian official. The Pulpit Commentary says this was not "cruel and haughty irony" but "simply of assumed resentment." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/44.htm)

**Baptist perspective (Garner-Howes):** "The brothers made their choice. Though they were appalled at the discovery of the incriminating cup in Benjamin's sack, they were unwilling to leave him to his fate. This was another step in the full cycle of their repentance." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-44.html)

---

### vv. 16–17 — Judah confesses guilt and offers all as slaves; Joseph refuses.

**Traditional Reading:** Judah's words — "God has found out the iniquity of your servants" — are the theological heart of the chapter. Guzik writes: "In Judah's mind, the brothers were now destined to live the rest of their lives as slaves in Egypt because they sold Joseph as a slave, some 20 years before this." The brothers were innocent of stealing the cup but guilty of far greater sins. Guzik adds: "Time does not erase the guilt of sin; only the blood of Jesus can." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-44/)

The Pulpit Commentary notes Judah does not refer to the cup-theft but to "some other iniquity… particularly the iniquity of selling Joseph." Gill likewise: "God hath found the iniquity of thy servants; brought it to their remembrance, fastened the guilt of it on their consciences." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/44.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/genesis-44.html)

Joseph refuses to enslave them all, insisting only Benjamin remain. Constable: "Joseph allowed Judah and the other brothers to depart and return home without Benjamin (44:17). However Judah's refusal to do so demonstrated the sincerity of the brothers' repentance." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-44.html)

---

### vv. 18–23 — Judah begins his plea, recounting the conversations with Joseph.

**Traditional Reading:** Judah's speech (vv.18-34) is widely regarded as one of the greatest passages in Scripture. Guzik cites F.B. Meyer ("In all literature, there is nothing more pathetic than this appeal"), H.C. Leupold ("one of the manliest, most straightforward speeches ever delivered"), and Donald Barnhouse ("the most moving address in all the Word of God"). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-44/)

The Pulpit Commentary describes it as "one of the masterpieces of Hebrew composition" and "one of the grandest and fairest to be found in the Old Testament." Its excellence lies in "the power of psychological truth, easy simplicity, and affecting pathos." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/44.htm)

Constable notes this is the longest speech in Genesis. Key repeated words: "servant" (10 times), "my lord" (7 times), and "father" (13 times). Martin Luther is quoted: "I would give very much to be able to pray before our Lord God as well as Judah prays here before Joseph. For this is a perfect pattern of prayer." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-44.html)

Judah begins with exquisite courtesy — "you are equal to Pharaoh himself" — acknowledging Joseph's absolute power to condemn or pardon. He reminds Joseph that it was the governor himself who initiated the questions about their family (v.19). Guzik observes: "Joseph must have inwardly smiled when he heard Judah say, of Benjamin, 'his brother is dead.' The brother he thought was dead stood right in front of them." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-44/)

---

### vv. 24–29 — Judah recounts the conversation with Jacob.

**Traditional Reading:** Judah now recounts Jacob's grief over Joseph and his terror at losing Benjamin. Ellicott notes the skill with which Judah mentions "the one went out from me" — the disappearance of one son explains the father's intense love for the remaining one. The allusion to Rachel ("my wife bore me two sons") would move Joseph's feelings, though Judah would not know this. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/44.htm)

Guzik highlights the delicate wording: "Judah did not say that Benjamin's brother was dead — only that Jacob said, 'Surely he is torn to pieces' and that Judah had not seen him since. Judah remembered the cruel lie that the brothers let their father believe regarding the death of Joseph." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-44/)

The phrase "bring down my gray hair to Sheol in sorrow" echoes Genesis 37:35. The Pulpit Commentary observes that Judah "with increased tenderness alludes to the touching lamentation of the stricken patriarch." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/44.htm)

---

### vv. 30–32 — Judah explains his personal stake: his life is bound up in the boy's.

**Traditional Reading:** Guzik notes the transformation: "More than 20 years before, Joseph's brothers didn't care about the pain they caused their father… Judah showed they were now greatly concerned for the feelings and welfare of their father." This is especially significant given how deeply Jacob's favouritism must have wounded Judah and the others over the years — yet his heart was changed to care even about the father who wounded them. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-44/)

Ellicott: "Judah first gives the reason why he was especially bound to see to Benjamin's welfare" — he had become surety (Genesis 43:9). Constable adds: "Judah manifested concern for Jacob as well as Benjamin (44:31). Rather than hating their father for favoring Joseph and then Benjamin, the brothers were now working for his welfare." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-44.html)

---

### vv. 33–34 — Judah offers himself as substitute for Benjamin.

**Traditional Reading:** This is the climax of the chapter — and of the entire Joseph narrative. Guzik writes: "Judah dramatically offered to lay down his life for the sake of Benjamin. This was a dramatic change from 22 years before when the brothers did not care about Joseph, Benjamin, or even their father Jacob." Judah was the very one who suggested selling Joseph into slavery (Genesis 37:26-27); now he offers to become a slave in Benjamin's place. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-44/)

The Pulpit Commentary calls this "sublime heroism": "In behalf of one whom he knew was preferred to a higher place in his father's affection than himself, he was willing to renounce his liberty." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/44.htm)

Constable: "The supreme proof of Judah's repentance, and the moral high point of his career, was his willingness to trade places with Benjamin and remain in Egypt as a slave (44:33-34; cf. John 15:13). This is the first instance of human substitution in Scripture (cf. Genesis 22:13)." He quotes Hamilton: "A spiritual metamorphosis for the better has certainly taken place in Judah… He who once callously engineered the selling of Joseph to strangers out of envy and anger is now willing to become Joseph's slave so that the rest of his brothers, and especially Benjamin [whom Jacob loved more than Judah], may be freed." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-44.html)

---

## DENOMINATIONAL EMPHASES

**Reformed / Presbyterian (John Piper / Desiring God):** Piper focuses on Judah's transformation as the key to understanding the whole Joseph story. He notes that Judah was the one who suggested selling Joseph (Gen 37:26-27), and his change culminates in Genesis 44. "Given the chance to dispense with Benjamin as the brothers did with Joseph, Judah offers himself as substitute. This leads, then, to his legacy." Piper connects this to kingly leadership: "Jacob will crown Judah with kingship (Genesis 49:10) because he demonstrates that he has become fit to rule according to God's ideal of kingship that the king serves the people, not vice versa." He also ties it to Christ: "Judah's pledge of safety and readiness to bear Benjamin's blame demonstrates love (instead of envy)… As Judah became a pledge of safety for his younger brother Benjamin, so the king in Israel should be a pledge of safety for his brothers and sisters." (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-legacy-of-good-leadership-is-sacrifice)

**Baptist (Garner-Howes):** Emphasises the testing of repentance. "Joseph arranged a final test to determine his brothers' attitude. He must determine if they were still the selfish, unloving, jealous brothers who once ignored his piteous pleas for mercy. Or were they indeed changed by genuine repentance." The conclusion: "The test was over. The brothers had been brought in deepest humility to recognize their past guilt… Now they were in a position for grace to come to their rescue. This principle is operative in all ages. 'God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace to the humble' (Jas 4:6)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-44.html)

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Guzik (whose site is listed under Pentecostal/charismatic sources) emphasises the emotional and relational transformation — the brothers' changed hearts evidenced in concrete actions: they didn't resent Benjamin's favoured portion, they trusted each other, they tore their clothes in horror, they stuck together, they humbled themselves, they acknowledged their sin, and Judah offered himself as a substitutionary sacrifice. Guzik draws a direct typological line to Christ: "This sacrificial love was perfectly displayed in Jesus Christ, the great descendant of Judah." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-44/)

**Lutheran:** Constable cites Martin Luther's commentary: "I would give very much to be able to pray before our Lord God as well as Judah prays here before Joseph. For this is a perfect pattern of prayer, yes, of the true feeling which should be in a prayer." This reflects the Lutheran emphasis on prayer as heartfelt appeal grounded in God's promises. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-44.html)

---

## OTHER VIEWS

**Modern Scholarship (Constable / NET Bible notes):** Constable, interacting with Waltke, Mathews, and Hamilton, highlights several technical points:
- The Hebrew verb *naḥash* in vv.5,15 is not the standard word for divination (*qasam*); it means "to whisper, mumble formulations, prophesy" (Leon Wood).
- The "cup" is *gabia‘* (chalice/goblet), not *kos* (ordinary cup).
- Judah's speech is analysed for its literary structure: key words "servant" (10×), "my lord" (7×), "father" (13×).
- This chapter presents "the first instance of human substitution in Scripture" — a literary-theological milestone.
- Waltke is quoted: "Judah is transformed from one who sells his brother as a slave to one who is willing to be the slave for his brother. With that offer he exemplifies Israel's ideal kingship." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-44.html)

**Catholic and Orthodox views:** No direct results were found from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org for Genesis 44 verse-by-verse commentary within the permitted searches. These sites tend to focus on dogmatic and liturgical resources rather than chapter-level Old Testament commentary.

**Debated modern teachings (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace):** No results were found from the permitted sites addressing Genesis 44 from these perspectives specifically.
